He ruled Mycenae at her side for years, until Agamemnon's grown son Orestes returned to avenge his father and slew them both, closing one more circle of the family's blood-curse.

orestes.name: Orestes
orestes.desc:
The son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, Orestes was bound by duty to avenge his murdered father — though the murderer was his own mother.

Driven by Apollo's command, he killed Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus, and for the crime of matricide was hounded across the world by the maddening Furies, until at last he was tried and absolved by Athena, breaking the ancient chain of vengeance.

electra.name: Electra
electra.desc:
A princess of Mycenae and daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, Electra nursed a burning hatred for the mother and lover who had murdered her father.

Living in grief and longing for vengeance, she kept her young brother Orestes safe and, when he returned grown, urged him on and stood with him in the killing of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus that avenged their father.

iphigenia.name: Iphigenia
iphigenia.desc:
A princess of Mycenae, daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, Iphigenia was sacrificed by her own father to appease Artemis and win fair winds for the Greek fleet bound for Troy. In some tellings the goddess snatched her from the altar at the last moment, leaving a deer in her place and carrying her off to serve as her priestess.

Her death sowed the hatred that drove Clytemnestra to murder Agamemnon.

cassandra.name: Cassandra
cassandra.desc:
A princess of Troy and daughter of Priam, Cassandra was granted the gift of prophecy by Apollo — but when she spurned him, he cursed the gift so that she would always speak the truth yet never be believed.

She foresaw the fall of Troy and warned against the Wooden Horse in vain, and after the city's fall was carried off by Agamemnon, foreseeing but powerless to prevent their shared murder in Mycenae.

hecuba.name: Hecuba
hecuba.desc:
The queen of Troy and wife of King Priam, Hecuba was mother to Hector, Paris, Cassandra and many of the city's princes. A figure of immense grief, she lived to see her husband and sons slain and her city destroyed.

Carried off into slavery after the fall, she took a terrible revenge on the king who murdered her last son, and in some tellings was transformed at last into a howling dog.

aeneas.name: Aeneas
aeneas.desc:
A prince of Troy and son of Aphrodite by the mortal Anchises, Aeneas was among the bravest of the Trojan defenders, second only to Hector. Protected by the gods, he survived the fall of the city, carrying his aged father on his back through the flames.

Fated to found a new nation, he led the Trojan survivors westward — and in Roman legend became the ancestor of Rome itself.

anchises.name: Anchises
anchises.desc:
A prince of the Trojan royal house, Anchises was a herdsman of such beauty that the goddess Aphrodite herself fell in love with him and bore him the hero Aeneas. Warned never to boast of the union, he let the secret slip and was struck lame by Zeus's thunderbolt for his pride.

When Troy fell, his son Aeneas carried him from the burning city upon his shoulders.

laomedon.name: Laomedon
laomedon.desc:
An early king of Troy and father of Priam, Laomedon was famed for his treachery. He cheated the gods Apollo and Poseidon of their wages after they built the city's walls, and later cheated Heracles of a promised reward for saving his daughter from a sea-monster.

For these broken oaths Heracles sacked Troy and slew him — a first fall that foreshadowed the city's final doom.

peleus.name: Peleus
peleus.desc:
A mortal hero and king of the Myrmidons, Peleus was the one man deemed worthy to wed the sea-nymph Thetis, given him when a prophecy warned that her son would surpass his father. Their wedding, attended by all the gods, was the very occasion of the golden Apple of Discord that sparked the Trojan War.

From their union came the greatest warrior of that war, Achilles.

telamon.name: Telamon
telamon.desc:
A mighty hero and king of Salamis, Telamon was a companion of Heracles and sailed with the Argonauts. He joined Heracles in the first sack of Troy under Laomedon, and was father to Ajax the Great, the towering bulwark of the Greeks in the later war.

A brother of Peleus, he belongs to the elder generation of heroes whose sons fought at Troy.

philoctetes.name: Philoctetes
philoctetes.desc:
A master archer and heir to the bow and poisoned arrows of Heracles, Philoctetes sailed for Troy but was bitten by a snake and abandoned by the Greeks on a desert island, his wound too foul to endure.

Left alone for ten years, he was fetched at last when a prophecy revealed that Troy could not fall without the bow of Heracles — and with it he helped bring the city down.

neoptolemus.name: Neoptolemus
neoptolemus.desc:
The son of Achilles, also called Pyrrhus, Neoptolemus was brought to Troy after his father's death, for a prophecy said the city could not fall without him.

Fierce and pitiless like his father, he was among the warriors hidden in the Wooden Horse, and cut down the aged King Priam at his own altar on the night the city burned.

palamedes.name: Palamedes
palamedes.desc:
A clever Greek hero credited with inventing letters, numbers and games, Palamedes was the man who exposed Odysseus's feigned madness when the hero tried to avoid the war.

Odysseus never forgave him, and later contrived his ruin — planting false evidence of treason so that Palamedes was stoned to death by the army, an innocent man destroyed by a rival's cunning.

anticlea.name: Anticlea
anticlea.desc:
The mother of Odysseus, Anticlea died of grief during her son's long absence, worn away by longing for his return.

When Odysseus journeyed to the land of the dead, he met her shade there and learned of her death and of the troubles besetting his home — and three times tried in vain to embrace her, his arms closing on empty air.

eurycleia.name: Eurycleia
eurycleia.desc:
The faithful old nurse of Odysseus, Eurycleia had raised the hero from infancy and kept watch over his household through his twenty-year absence.

When he returned in disguise, it was she who recognised him — by the old scar on his thigh as she washed his feet — and kept his secret until the very moment of his revenge upon the suitors.

argos_dog.name: Argos
argos_dog.desc:
The faithful hound of Odysseus, Argos was a strong young dog when his master sailed for Troy, and lay neglected and flea-ridden on a dung-heap through the twenty years of his absence.

When Odysseus at last returned in beggar's disguise, Argos alone knew him at once — and having lived only to see his master once more, the old dog wagged his tail, dropped his ears, and died.

aeolus.name: Aeolus
aeolus.desc:
The keeper of the winds, Aeolus dwelt on a floating island where he held the four winds captive, loosing them at the will of the gods.

When Odysseus came to him, he gave the hero a leather bag holding all the storm-winds, that only the gentle west wind might carry him home — but his crew, thinking it treasure, opened the bag and loosed the tempest that blew them far off course.

elpenor.name: Elpenor
elpenor.desc:
The youngest of Odysseus's crew, Elpenor met an inglorious end — falling drunk from the roof of Circe's hall and breaking his neck.

Unburied and forgotten in the haste of departure, his was the first shade Odysseus met in the underworld, begging that his body be given proper burial so his spirit could find rest.

eurylochus.name: Eurylochus
eurylochus.desc:
A kinsman and second-in-command to Odysseus, Eurylochus is a cautious and sometimes mutinous figure among the crew. It was he who prudently held back when Circe turned his companions to swine, escaping to warn Odysseus.

But it was also he who persuaded the starving men to slaughter the forbidden cattle of the sun — the sacrilege that doomed them all.

graeae.name: The Graeae
graeae.desc:
Three grey sisters, ancient from their very birth, the Graeae shared between them a single eye and a single tooth, which they passed from hand to hand.

Sisters and guardians of the Gorgons, they were outwitted by the hero Perseus, who snatched their shared eye as it passed and would not return it until they told him the way to find Medusa and the weapons he needed.

stheno.name: Stheno
stheno.desc:
The eldest of the three Gorgon sisters, Stheno was — unlike her mortal sister Medusa — an immortal monster, with serpents for hair and a face that turned onlookers to stone.

Said to be the most ferocious and murderous of the three, she survived the raid in which Perseus beheaded Medusa, and with her sister Euryale pursued the fleeing hero in vain.

euryale.name: Euryale
euryale.desc:
One of the three immortal Gorgon sisters, Euryale shared with her sisters serpent hair and a petrifying gaze.

Famed for her terrible, far-carrying cry, she let out a great bellow of grief and rage when the hero Perseus beheaded her mortal sister Medusa — and, being immortal, she could not be slain in turn.

geryon.name: Geryon
geryon.desc:
A monstrous giant with three bodies joined at the waist, Geryon dwelt on a far western island where he kept a famous herd of red cattle, guarded by the two-headed hound Orthrus and a herdsman.

The seizing of these cattle was the tenth labour of Heracles, who sailed to the world's edge, killed the hound and the herdsman, and slew the three-bodied giant with a single venom-steeped arrow.

orthrus.name: Orthrus
orthrus.desc:
A monstrous two-headed hound, Orthrus was the brother of Cerberus, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, set to guard the red cattle of the giant Geryon on his far western isle.

When Heracles came for the herd as his tenth labour, the great hound rushed him and was struck down by a single blow of the hero's club, before Heracles turned upon Geryon himself.

talos.name: Talos
talos.desc:
A giant man of living bronze, Talos was the guardian of Crete, forged to circle the island three times a day and hurl boulders at any approaching ships. A single vein of ichor ran through his body, sealed by a bronze pin at his ankle.

When the Argonauts came, the sorceress Medea beguiled him and drew the pin, so that the divine fluid drained away and the bronze giant toppled lifeless.

erymanthian_boar.name: Erymanthian Boar
erymanthian_boar.desc:
A gigantic and savage wild boar that ravaged the region of Mount Erymanthus, this beast was the target of the fourth labour of Heracles.

Rather than kill it, the hero was charged to bring it back alive — which he did by chasing the exhausted boar into deep snow, binding it fast, and carrying it back on his shoulders to the terror of King Eurystheus.

stymphalian_birds.name: Stymphalian Birds
stymphalian_birds.desc:
A flock of man-eating birds with beaks, claws and feathers of bronze, the Stymphalian Birds infested a marsh in Arcadia, where they had bred out of all control.

Driving them from their cover was the sixth labour of Heracles, who startled the whole flock into the air with a great bronze rattle given him by Athena, then shot them down with his arrows as they scattered in fright.

ceryneian_hind.name: Ceryneian Hind
ceryneian_hind.desc:
An enormous deer sacred to the goddess Artemis, the Ceryneian Hind had golden horns and hooves of bronze, and could outrun an arrow in flight.

To capture it alive without harming it was the third labour of Heracles, who pursued the tireless creature for a full year across the world before catching it at last — taking care to appease the goddess whose sacred animal it was.

cretan_bull.name: Cretan Bull
cretan_bull.desc:
A magnificent and savage bull that rampaged across the island of Crete, this was the very beast that had fathered the Minotaur upon Queen Pasiphae.

Its capture was the seventh labour of Heracles, who wrestled it into submission and carried it back alive — after which it was set loose to roam again, until it was finally slain by the hero Theseus at Marathon.

colchian_dragon.name: Colchian Dragon
colchian_dragon.desc:
A monstrous, sleepless serpent, the Colchian Dragon was set to guard the Golden Fleece where it hung in a sacred grove in distant Colchis.

When Jason and the Argonauts came for the prize, the beast could not be overcome by force — until the sorceress Medea lulled it into an enchanted sleep with her potions and songs, allowing Jason to seize the Fleece at last.

ino.name: Ino
ino.desc:
A princess of Thebes and sister of Semele, Ino helped to raise the infant Dionysus, drawing down the fury of Hera.

Driven mad by the goddess, she leapt into the sea with her young son in her arms — but rather than perish, the two were transformed into merciful sea-deities: Ino became Leucothea, the White Goddess, who aids sailors in distress, and who once saved the drowning Odysseus with her veil.

agave.name: Agave
agave.desc:
A princess of Thebes and mother of King Pentheus, Agave denied that her nephew Dionysus was truly a god.

For this the god struck her and her sisters with ecstatic madness and drove them to the mountains as maenads — where, in their frenzy, she tore apart her own son Pentheus, bearing his head home in triumph before the horror of the deed broke upon her.

pentheus.name: Pentheus
pentheus.desc:
The young king of Thebes who denied the divinity of Dionysus, Pentheus tried to ban the god's ecstatic rites and imprison him.

In revenge, Dionysus lured him to spy on the frenzied maenads in the mountains — where, in their god-sent madness, they took him for a wild beast and tore him limb from limb, his own mother Agave leading the slaughter with his head in her hands.

actaeon.name: Actaeon
actaeon.desc:
A young hunter of Thebes, Actaeon met a terrible fate for an innocent trespass. Wandering the woods, he chanced upon the goddess Artemis bathing naked in a pool — and the outraged virgin goddess, to punish him for the sight, transformed him into a stag.

Fleeing in terror, he was set upon by his own fifty hunting hounds, who failed to know their master and tore him to pieces.

eteocles.name: Eteocles
eteocles.desc:
A prince of Thebes and son of Oedipus, Eteocles agreed to share the throne with his brother Polynices in alternate years — then refused to yield when his own turn was done.

His brother marched against the city with a foreign army in the war of the Seven against Thebes, and the two met in single combat at the gates and killed each other, fulfilling their father's curse.

polynices.name: Polynices
polynices.desc:
A prince of Thebes and son of Oedipus, Polynices was cheated of his agreed turn upon the throne by his brother Eteocles. Raising a foreign army, he led the doomed war of the Seven against Thebes to reclaim his right, and met his brother in single combat at the city gates, where each slew the other.

It was the ban on his burial that set the tragedy of Antigone in motion.

creon.name: Creon
creon.desc:
The king of Thebes after the fall of Oedipus, Creon set the rigid law of the state against the older law of the gods.

Forbidding the burial of his nephew as a traitor, he condemned Antigone to death for defying him — and was punished by the loss of his own son and wife, learning too late the cost of his unbending pride.

ismene.name: Ismene
ismene.desc:
A princess of Thebes and the gentler sister of Antigone, Ismene shrank from defying King Creon's edict against burying their brother, counselling caution and obedience. Though she later offered to share her bolder sister's punishment, Antigone refused her the sacrifice.

She survives as the quieter foil to Antigone's uncompromising courage — the sister who chose to live.

haemon.name: Haemon
haemon.desc:
A prince of Thebes and son of King Creon, Haemon was betrothed to his cousin Antigone.

When his father condemned her to death for burying her brother against his edict, Haemon pleaded desperately for her life in vain — and, finding her dead in her tomb, he took his own life beside her body, a loss that helped to break his tyrant father.

links.details: Out of the first yawning Chaos, Gaia the deep-rooted Earth arose of her own accord — not born but simply coming to be, the first firm ground in a formless void and the foundation on which all later creation would rest.

Nyx, primordial Night, was among the very first beings to arise from Chaos, the yawning void at the beginning of all things. She emerged needing no parent in the ordinary sense — a firstborn power of the cosmos, older than the gods, from whom Day and Death and Sleep would all descend.
Erebus, the underworld's darkness, emerged from Chaos beside his sister Night.
Tartarus, the pit beneath the earth, came into being with Chaos — one day the prison of the Titans.
Gaia the Earth brought forth Uranus the Sky of her own accord and made him her equal and mate — the first divine union — before she turned against his cruelty and armed their son to unmake him.
Gaia the Earth brought forth Pontus the Sea from herself without a father, and from their union descended the ancient sea-gods — Nereus, Phorcys, Ceto and their monstrous brood.

Uranus fathered Cronus among the twelve Titans, then hated and imprisoned his monstrous children within the earth — until Cronus, armed by Gaia with a sickle, unmanned his father and seized the throne of heaven for himself.

Enraged that Uranus imprisoned her monstrous children in her own depths, Gaia forged a great sickle of grey flint and begged her Titan sons to punish their father. Only Cronus, the youngest, dared: at his mother's urging he lay in ambush and castrated Uranus, seizing the heavens for himself.

So Gaia set in motion the first overthrow of the cosmos — a mother arming a son against a father, the pattern the whole succession myth would repeat.
Rhea, daughter of Uranus, would become the mother of the Olympians.
Gaia's daughter Rhea would repeat her mother's trick — helping a son overthrow a devouring father.
Oceanus, eldest of the Titans and the world-encircling river, is a son of Uranus the Sky and Gaia the Earth.
Gaia's son Oceanus stayed neutral in the war of the gods, and kept his ancient waters.
Tethys the Titaness is a daughter of Uranus and Gaia, and wife to her brother Oceanus.
Gaia's daughter Tethys bore the three thousand rivers and ocean-nymphs.
Hyperion, Titan of light and father of Sun, Moon and Dawn, is a son of Uranus and Gaia.
Gaia's son Hyperion fathered the very lights of the sky.
Theia, Titaness of light, is a daughter of Uranus and Gaia and mother of the sky's lights.
Gaia's daughter Theia mothered the Sun, Moon and Dawn.
Themis, Titaness of divine law, is a daughter of Uranus and Gaia.
Gaia's daughter Themis embodied the old order of custom and right.
Mnemosyne, Memory, is a daughter of Uranus and Gaia, and will mother the nine Muses.
Gaia the Earth bore the Titaness Mnemosyne, Memory, whose daughters by Zeus are the Muses.
Iapetus the Titan, father of Atlas and Prometheus, is a son of Uranus and Gaia.
Gaia's son Iapetus fathered a line of rebels against Olympus.
Coeus, Titan of the inquiring mind, is a son of Uranus and Gaia.
Gaia's son Coeus, whose line carried the gift of prophecy.
Phoebe, Titaness of prophecy, is a daughter of Uranus and Gaia.
Gaia's daughter Phoebe passed her prophetic power down to Leto and Apollo.
Coeus fathered Leto upon his sister Phoebe, making the Titan of the heavenly axis grandfather to Apollo and Artemis.
Phoebe's daughter Leto carried the family's prophetic gift to the next generation.

Metis was a daughter of Oceanus, the vast world-encircling river, and Tethys — one of the Oceanids, and the wisest of them. From her Titan parents she inherited the deep, fluid cunning that made her the cleverest of the early powers, the counsellor even Zeus needed and feared.
Tethys bore Metis, whose cunning wisdom Zeus coveted enough to consume.
Atlas, condemned to hold up the sky, is a son of the Titan Iapetus.
Iapetus fathered Prometheus, the cunning Titan of forethought whose theft of fire and defence of mortal men would openly defy the order of Zeus.

Warned that a son would one day cast him down just as he had cast down his own father Uranus, Cronus swallowed each of his children whole the moment they were born — Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, one after another. But when Zeus came, his mother Rhea hid the infant away on Crete and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling to gulp down in his place. Grown in secret, Zeus returned to force his father to disgorge the swallowed gods — alive and full-grown — and led them in the war that toppled the Titans.
Rhea smuggled the newborn Zeus to a Cretan cave and gave Cronus a swaddled stone to swallow in his place.
Cronus swallowed the infant Hera whole, fearing the prophecy that a child of his would unseat him.
Rhea's daughter Hera, disgorged from Cronus, would reign as queen of the order that replaced him.
Cronus swallowed Poseidon at birth; Zeus later made him bring the sea-god back up whole.
Rhea's son Poseidon drew the sea when the three brothers divided the cosmos by lot.
Cronus devoured Hades as an infant, as he did all Rhea's children.
Rhea's eldest son Hades drew the underworld when the brothers cast lots for the world.
Cronus swallowed Demeter, the harvest-goddess-to-be, at her birth.
Rhea's daughter Demeter would make the earth fruitful — or, in her grief, barren.
Hestia was the first child Cronus swallowed and the last he disgorged — 'first and last', as her hearth-cult put it.
Rhea's eldest daughter Hestia chose the quiet hearth over a throne among the squabbling gods.

Warned that the child of the wise Titaness Metis would one day surpass him, Zeus swallowed her whole while she was still pregnant. But the child grew on inside him, until a blinding headache split his skull — Hephaestus struck it open with an axe, and out sprang Athena, full-grown and clad in armour, with a war-cry that shook Olympus. She became the favourite Zeus trusts above all his children: keeper of his aegis, and the only other hand he ever lets close on the thunderbolt.

Warned that any son born to Metis would overthrow him, Zeus swallowed the pregnant Titaness whole — but her wisdom passed into him, and the child grew inside his skull. When the pain became unbearable, Hephaestus split Zeus's head with an axe and Athena sprang out fully armed, shouting a war-cry.

So Metis is Athena's mother in the strangest of senses: swallowed before the birth, she gave her daughter both her craft and her cunning, and lives on as the counsel Zeus is said to carry within him.
Apollo, archer-god of prophecy and plague, is the son of Zeus by the Titaness Leto.
Hounded across the world by a jealous Hera, Leto at last bore Apollo on the floating isle of Delos.
Artemis the huntress is the daughter of Zeus by Leto, and twin sister of Apollo.
Leto bore Artemis on Delos, and the newborn goddess is said to have helped her mother deliver her twin Apollo.
Ares, Zeus's son by Hera — and the child Zeus openly calls the most hateful of all the gods.
Ares is Hera's son by Zeus — the war-god she alone among the Olympians favours.
Hephaestus the smith is a son of Zeus and Hera, cast from Olympus as a child and lamed by the fall.
Hera bore Hephaestus without a father and, disgusted by his lameness, flung the infant from heaven — a rejection he never forgets.
Hermes the quick-witted messenger is the son of Zeus by the Pleiad Maia.
The shy nymph Maia bore Hermes to Zeus in a mountain cave; the infant stole Apollo's cattle before his first nightfall.
Zeus fathered Persephone on Demeter — then promised her, unasked, to his brother Hades.
Persephone is the daughter of Demeter, whose loss to Hades froze the whole earth in her mother's grief.
When his mortal mother died, Zeus sewed the unborn Dionysus into his own thigh and carried him to term.
Dionysus was carried to term in Zeus's own thigh after his mortal mother Semele was burned to ash.

When Cronus castrated Uranus and flung the severed parts into the sea, the immortal flesh churned the waves into white foam, and from that foam rose Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty, stepping ashore fully grown. So the goddess of desire was born from an act of violence against the sky-father — beauty out of the wound of the old order.
Maia, eldest of Atlas's daughters the Pleiades, hid in a cave and there bore Zeus the god Hermes.
Gaia the Earth and Uranus the Sky, the first married pair, until Gaia turned their son Cronus against a husband who buried her children.

Nyx, primordial Night, and Erebus, the darkness of the underworld, were among the first beings to emerge from Chaos, and from their union came Aether the bright upper air and Hemera the Day — light born, strangely, out of the deepest dark. Nyx is a power even Zeus is said to fear, dwelling at the edge of the world where Night and Day pass each other at the threshold.
Cronus took his sister Rhea as his consort and queen through the golden age of the Titans — until his devouring of their children drove her to hide the infant Zeus and end his reign.
Oceanus the world-river and his Titaness wife Tethys, parents of every river and three thousand ocean-nymphs.
Hyperion and Theia, two Titans of light, whose union produced Helios the Sun, Selene the Moon and Eos the Dawn.
Coeus and Phoebe, Titans of intellect and prophecy, grandparents of Apollo and Artemis through their daughter Leto.
Zeus and Hera, king and queen of the gods, locked in a marriage of endless quarrels over his affairs and her furious revenge.

As Persephone gathered flowers in a meadow the earth split open, and Hades burst up in his black chariot to seize her down into the land of the dead. Her mother Demeter wandered the world in grief and let every crop wither until Zeus commanded the girl's return — but Hades had tricked her into eating pomegranate seeds, and whoever tastes the food of the dead can never wholly leave it. So Persephone reigns beside him a third of each year, and for as long as she is gone the world withers into winter and waits for her.

The lame smith Hephaestus was wedded to Aphrodite, goddess of desire — a marriage she honoured little, taking Ares the war-god as her lover. Warned by the all-seeing Sun, Hephaestus forged a net of bronze links so fine as to be invisible and strung it above his bed. When the lovers lay down together, the net dropped and bound them fast, and Hephaestus flung open the doors and called in all the gods to laugh at the pair caught naked and helpless — his revenge not violence, but ridicule.
Laertes is the father of Odysseus; aged and grieving, he withdraws to his orchard and does not learn his son still lives until the very end.

For the twenty years Odysseus was gone — ten at Troy, ten lost at sea — Penelope held Ithaca and their marriage together against a house full of suitors. She promised to choose a new husband once she finished weaving a shroud for old Laertes, then unpicked her day's work each night, holding them off for three years by the trick.

When Odysseus finally returned in disguise, it was Penelope who set the test of the great bow, and Penelope who tested him in turn — asking about their marriage bed, carved from a living olive tree, a secret only the true Odysseus could know. Their reunion is the still centre the whole Odyssey travels toward.
Odysseus left Telemachus an infant when he sailed for Troy, and returned twenty years later to a grown son who fought at his side to reclaim their home.

Telemachus was the infant Penelope was left to raise alone when Odysseus sailed for Troy, and by the time his father returned he had grown into a young man goaded past patience by the suitors devouring his inheritance. Mother and son held the household between them through the long wait, and it was to Telemachus that Odysseus first revealed himself, the two of them plotting the suitors' end together.
Helen was Zeus's daughter by Leda — her mortal beauty the divine spark that set Greece and Troy at war.
Menelaus is the husband of Helen, whose flight to Troy with Paris launched a thousand ships and a ten-year war to win her back.

Polyphemus was Poseidon's son, and when Odysseus blinded the Cyclops and taunted him with his true name, the giant prayed to his father for vengeance. Poseidon answered: he could not stop Odysseus reaching home, but he could make the journey a torment of storms and shipwreck, and swore that the hero would arrive late, alone, broken, and to a house full of trouble.

That curse is the engine of the Odyssey — a father's grief for a maimed son turned into ten years of the wine-dark sea.
Nausicaa is the level-headed daughter of King Alcinous of the Phaeacians, whose kindness sets the shipwrecked Odysseus on his last road home.
Athena adores Odysseus for his cunning — a match of two sharp minds. She disguises, guides and defends him at every turn of the journey home.
Athena, disguised as old Mentor, stiffens young Telemachus and sends him off in search of his father Odysseus.
Hermes hands Odysseus the herb moly to resist Circe's magic, and later carries Zeus's order that frees him from Calypso.
For blinding his son Polyphemus, Poseidon dogs Odysseus with storm and shipwreck across ten years of sea.

Trapped in the Cyclops's cave and watched as his men were eaten two at a time, Odysseus gave his name as 'Nobody,' got Polyphemus drunk on strong wine, and drove a sharpened, fire-hardened stake into his single eye. When the blinded giant roared for help, his neighbours asked who was hurting him; 'Nobody,' he bellowed, and they left him to it.

Odysseus and his men escaped clinging beneath the rams. But pride undid the trick: sailing away, Odysseus shouted back his real name — and gave Polyphemus the means to curse him to his divine father.
Forced to choose, Odysseus steers close to six-headed Scylla rather than the whirlpool — and knowingly loses six men to her jaws.
Odysseus barely survives the whirlpool Charybdis twice, once clinging to a fig tree above it as it swallows his broken raft.

The Sirens sang so sweetly that sailors steered onto their rocks to listen and died there among the bones of earlier fools. Forewarned by Circe, Odysseus had his crew stop their ears with beeswax and lash him to the mast — leaving his own ears open, the one man to hear the song and live.

As the ship passed he strained and begged to be untied, and his deaf crew, obeying his earlier orders, only bound him tighter until the deadly music faded astern.
When the starving crew slaughter Helios's sacred cattle against explicit warning, Zeus's thunderbolt destroys the ship and drowns every man but Odysseus.

Landing on Aeaea, Odysseus's scouts were welcomed by the enchantress Circe — who fed them, then touched them with her wand and turned them into swine. Warned by Hermes and armed with the herb moly against her magic, Odysseus resisted the spell, drew his sword, and forced her to restore his men. Won over, Circe kept him a year in comfort and love, and when at last he pressed to leave, it was she who told him he must first sail to the land of the dead to learn his way home.

Cast up alone on the island of Ogygia, Odysseus was taken in by the nymph Calypso, who loved him and kept him seven years — offering him immortality and eternal youth if he would only stay and be her husband. But each day he sat weeping on the shore, gazing across the sea toward Ithaca and the wife he could not forget. At last Zeus sent Hermes to command his release, and Calypso, grieving, helped him build the raft that bore him away from her deathless love.
Summoned from the dead, the blind seer Tiresias laid out for Odysseus the whole road home — and the one temptation, Helios's cattle, that would doom his crew.
The old horseman Nestor received Telemachus warmly at Pylos, but had only war-stories and a send-off to Sparta.
At Sparta, Menelaus told Telemachus what he had wrung from the sea-god Proteus: that Odysseus still lived, held on Calypso's isle.
Helios the Sun demanded justice for his slaughtered cattle, threatening to shine among the dead, and Zeus obliged with the thunderbolt that wrecked Odysseus's ship.
King Alcinous of the Phaeacians feasted the stranger Odysseus, heard his whole tale, and gave him the ship that finally landed him on Ithaca.
Nausicaa found the shipwrecked Odysseus naked on the beach, clothed and fed him, and pointed him to her father's hall.
The swineherd Eumaeus sheltered his ragged, disguised master Odysseus, proving the loyalty that helped him retake the house.
Antinous, ringleader of the suitors, gorged on Odysseus's stores while pressing Penelope to remarry — and was first to fall to the returning king's bow.

Home at last after twenty years, disguised as a ragged beggar, Odysseus found his hall overrun by suitors devouring his wealth and pressing his wife to remarry — chief among them the arrogant Antinous. When Penelope set the test of the great bow that only Odysseus could string, the beggar alone bent and strung it, then turned it on the crowd. His first arrow took Antinous through the throat as the suitor raised a cup to drink, and the slaughter of the whole company began.

Hector was Priam's eldest son and Troy's great defender, and when Achilles killed him and dragged his body behind a chariot, the old king did the unthinkable: he went alone at night into the enemy camp, knelt before the man who had slaughtered his son, and kissed the hands that had done it, begging for the body back.

That meeting — grief recognising grief, Achilles thinking of his own father — is the moral heart of the Iliad, and it wins Hector the funeral Troy gives him in the poem's final lines.

Paris was the son a prophecy warned would bring Troy's ruin, exposed at birth but raised to manhood after all. It was his abduction of Helen that brought the Greek armies to Priam's walls, and though the old king never cast him out, it was Paris's act that doomed the city, Priam's other sons, and Priam himself.
Hector and Andromache share the Iliad's most tender scene — his farewell at the gates, their infant son frightened by his plumed helmet — before he goes out to die.
The two sons of Atreus; Menelaus's stolen wife is the cause Agamemnon leads a thousand ships to avenge.
The brave brother and the reckless one — Hector fights the war Paris started, and barely hides his contempt for him.

The sea-nymph Thetis, married against her will to the mortal Peleus, tried to make their son immortal by dipping the infant Achilles in the river Styx — holding him by the heel, the one spot the waters never touched. Knowing he was fated to die young at Troy, she hid him among girls to keep him from the war, and grieved openly once he chose glory over long life.

Even in his rage and mourning she came to him from the sea, brought him divine armour forged by Hephaestus, and wept for the short bright span she could not save.

Promised the most beautiful woman in the world by Aphrodite — his reward for naming her fairest of the three goddesses — Paris sailed to Sparta as a guest of King Menelaus and carried off his wife, Helen, the face that would launch a thousand ships. Whether she went willingly or was seized, the theft shattered the sacred bond between host and guest and gave the kings of Greece their cause for war. For ten years the united armies of Achaea besieged Troy to win her back.
Athena stays Achilles' hand from killing Agamemnon in council, and later tricks Hector into standing his ground to die.
Hera, who loathes Troy, backs the Greek commander Agamemnon throughout the war.
Poseidon, no friend of Troy, guards the Greek champion Achilles on the field.
Aphrodite snatched her favourite Paris out of certain death in his duel with Menelaus, hiding him in a cloud.
Apollo shielded Troy's champion Hector through the fighting — until the fatal day he abandoned him to Achilles.
The war-god Ares himself took the field on the Trojan side beside Hector.
Athena fills Diomedes with such fury she lets him wound the gods — and personally steers his spear into Ares.

Patroclus, Achilles's dearest companion, could not bear to watch the Greeks slaughtered while his friend sulked in his tent. He begged to wear Achilles's own armour and lead his men, and the sight of it drove the Trojans back in terror — until Patroclus, forgetting his promise not to press too far, charged the walls. There Apollo struck the helm from his head, a spear found his back, and Hector ran him through, stripping the borrowed armour from his body. It was this death that would bring Achilles roaring back into the war.

When Hector killed Patroclus, Achilles's grief curdled into a fury that drove him back into the war he had forsworn. He chased Hector three times around the walls of Troy before the gods stayed the Trojan's flight, then ran him through the throat. Deaf to Hector's dying plea for burial, he lashed the body to his chariot and dragged it in the dust beneath the city walls — until old King Priam came alone by night to his tent to beg his son back, and Achilles, weeping for his own father, at last relented.

For all his fury and half-divine strength, Achilles could be wounded in only one place: the heel by which his mother Thetis had held him as she dipped him in the river Styx. In the tenth year of the war, as he stormed the very gates of Troy, Paris — no great warrior, but an archer — loosed an arrow, and Apollo guided it. It struck Achilles in that one mortal heel, and the greatest of the Greeks fell at last, killed not in single combat but by a bowshot from the walls.
Apollo guides Paris's arrow to Achilles' heel, letting Troy's destroyer be destroyed in turn.

Achilles and Patroclus were bound closer than brothers, raised together and inseparable at Troy. When Patroclus fell to Hector while wearing Achilles' own armour, grief drove Achilles back into a war he had abandoned — and his vengeance sealed his own doom.
The old king Nestor's counsel is long-winded but sound; he begs Agamemnon again and again to make peace with Achilles.
Odysseus's diplomacy holds the fracturing Greek army together whenever Agamemnon's blunders threaten to break it.

Briseis was a captive woman awarded to Achilles as his prize of honour after the sack of her city — where he had killed her husband and brothers. When a plague forced Agamemnon to give up his own captive, the great king seized Briseis from Achilles instead, to salve his wounded pride. It was this insult — the theft of his rightful prize — that drove Achilles into the furious sulk that kept him from the war, and cost the Greeks so dearly before his grief for Patroclus brought him back.
At the plea of Thetis, Hephaestus forged for Achilles a shield and armour blazing with the whole world worked in miniature.
Achilles and Agamemnon quarrel over a captive woman, and really over honour — the wound the whole Iliad turns on.
Great Ajax and Hector duel to an honourable standstill, then trade gifts in mutual respect — a rare courtesy in this war.
Diomedes speared the hand of Aphrodite as she carried her son from the field, and sent the goddess weeping back to Olympus.
With Athena driving his spear, Diomedes wounded the war-god Ares himself, who fled the field bellowing to Zeus.
Heracles is the mortal son of Zeus by Alcmene — the half-divine strength that lets him survive Hera's lifelong hatred.
Alcmene bore Heracles to Zeus, who had come to her disguised as her own husband.
Hera hounds Heracles from the cradle — serpents in his crib, then the madness in which he kills his own children, the crime the Twelve Labours must expiate.

For his first labour Heracles was sent against the Nemean Lion, a beast whose golden hide no weapon on earth could pierce — arrows glanced away, blades bent against it. Seeing that steel was useless, he cornered the lion in its cave, seized it in his bare arms, and throttled the life from it. Then, since no knife could cut the pelt, he skinned it with the beast's own razor claws, and wore that impenetrable hide ever after as cloak and armour.

The second labour set Heracles against the Lernaean Hydra, a serpent whose blood was deadly poison and whose heads, when struck off, grew back doubled. As he fought, Hera sent a great crab to bite his heel, but he crushed it underfoot. Seeing he could never win by the blade alone, he had his nephew Iolaus sear each severed neck with fire so no new head could rise, and buried the one immortal head beneath a boulder. He dipped his arrows in her venom, and they carried death ever after.

For his eleventh labour Heracles sought the golden apples of the Hesperides, which grew in a far garden guarded by Ladon — a hundred-headed dragon that never slept, coiled around the tree. Some tales say Heracles shot the dragon dead over the garden wall with an arrow steeped in Hydra's venom; others that he sent Atlas to fetch the apples while he took the weight of the sky upon his own shoulders, and tricked the Titan into taking it back. Either way the deathless apples were won.

For his twelfth and final labour, Heracles was sent down into the underworld to fetch Cerberus himself — the three-headed hound, serpent-tailed, that guards the gate so no shade may leave. Hades gave him leave to take the beast on one condition: that he master it with his bare hands and use no weapon. Heracles seized the monster by its throats, endured its bites and its serpent-sting, and wrestled it up into the light of day — then, the labour done, carried it back down and set it once more at its post.
Iolaus, nephew and charioteer of Heracles, seared the Hydra's necks — the help that made his uncle's impossible Labour possible.
Deianira is the third wife of Heracles, whose jealous 'love-charm' becomes the poison that destroys him.

Deianira loved Heracles and never meant to kill him. Long before, the dying centaur Nessus — slain by Heracles for assaulting her — had given her his blood as a false love-charm, swearing it would hold her husband faithful. Years later, fearing a rival, she soaked a robe in it and sent it to him. But the blood was fouled with the Hydra's venom from Heracles's own arrow; it burned into his flesh like fire and could not be torn free. In agony he built his own pyre, and Deianira, learning what she had done, took her life.
It was Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, who set Heracles the twelve labours — and hid in a bronze jar from the monsters the hero brought back.

For all his suffering, Heracles's death was not an end. As the poisoned robe burned him alive upon his pyre, the mortal part of him was consumed, but the divine part — his father Zeus's share — rose to Olympus, where he was welcomed at last among the gods and reconciled even with Hera, who had hounded him all his life. There he was given the goddess Hebe, eternal youth herself, as his immortal bride — his rest and reward after a lifetime of labours.

Zeus desired Alcmene, the virtuous wife of Amphitryon, but she would yield to no one but her husband. So while the real Amphitryon was away at war, Zeus took his exact shape and came to her — and to lengthen their union he commanded the sun not to rise, holding back the dawn for three days. From that long night was conceived Heracles, mightiest of all heroes; and when the true Amphitryon returned the following night, Alcmene bore twin sons — the god's, and the mortal's.
Perseus is the son of Zeus, who reached the imprisoned Danae as a shower of gold.
Locked in a bronze room to thwart a prophecy, Danae bore Perseus to Zeus and was cast adrift with him in a chest.

Danae's father Acrisius, warned by an oracle that his daughter's son would one day kill him, shut her away in a chamber of bronze where no man could reach her. But Zeus came to her as a shower of golden rain, pouring down through the roof into her lap, and she conceived the hero Perseus. When Acrisius found the child, he could not kill his own blood outright, and set mother and baby adrift in a wooden chest upon the sea — from which they were saved, and the prophecy only delayed.

Sent to fetch the head of the Gorgon Medusa — an errand meant to be his death — Perseus was armed by the gods: the winged sandals of Hermes, the cap of invisibility from Hades, and Athena's mirror-bright shield. Because Medusa's gaze turned the living to stone, he crept up watching only her reflection, and struck her head off as she slept. From the severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, and Perseus flew away with the head sealed in a bag — a weapon whose petrifying stare he would yet turn against his enemies.

Andromeda had been chained to the rocks as a sacrifice to Cetus, the sea-monster Poseidon had sent to punish her mother's boast. As the vast beast surged from the deep to devour her, Perseus — flying home on winged sandals with Medusa's head in his bag — swooped down upon it. Some say he showed the monster the Gorgon's petrifying face; most that he plunged his blade again and again into its flesh until the sea ran red, and freed the princess to make her his bride.

Flying home with Medusa's head, Perseus found Andromeda chained to a sea-cliff — offered up to a monster sent by Poseidon because her mother Cassiopeia had boasted of a beauty greater than the sea-nymphs'. As the beast surged from the waves he swooped down and slew it, then claimed the princess as his bride. When her former betrothed came with armed men to seize her, Perseus lifted the Gorgon's head, and turned the whole wedding-hall to stone.
Athena lends Perseus her polished shield so he can strike Medusa by reflection, never meeting her eyes.
Hermes equips Perseus with the winged sandals and the adamantine sickle for the Gorgon's neck.

Medusa was once a beautiful maiden, a priestess in Athena's temple — until Poseidon violated her in that very sanctuary. Athena, unable or unwilling to punish the god, turned her wrath upon the victim: she transformed Medusa's lovely hair into a nest of hissing serpents and made her face so dreadful that any who met her gaze were turned to stone. Cast out and monstrous, Medusa dwelt at the world's edge until Perseus came for her head — which Athena then set upon her own shield.
From the blood of Medusa's severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus.
The sea-monster Cetus was sent to devour Andromeda in payment for her mother's boast, until Perseus turned it to stone.
On the oracle's word, King Cepheus chained his own daughter Andromeda to the rock for the monster.
Cassiopeia's boast that she outshone the sea-nymphs is what doomed her daughter Andromeda to the rock.
Cepheus and Cassiopeia, king and queen of Aethiopia, whose pride nearly cost them their daughter Andromeda.
Aegeus left tokens under a rock for the son he'd secretly fathered; the grown Theseus lifted it and came to claim Athens.
By another account Theseus was Poseidon's son — the sea-god's blood behind his heroics.

Every nine years Athens was forced to send seven youths and seven maidens into the Cretan Labyrinth, to be devoured by the Minotaur — the bull-headed monster penned at its heart. Theseus went among them of his own will, and Ariadne, the Cretan princess who had fallen in love with him, secretly gave him a ball of thread to unwind as he walked. Deep in the maze he found the Minotaur and killed it with his bare hands, then followed the thread back to the entrance — the only soul ever to enter the Labyrinth and come out alive.

Ariadne, daughter of King Minos, fell in love with Theseus the moment she saw him among the youths sent to feed the Minotaur, and gave him the thread that let him find his way out of the Labyrinth after the kill. She fled Crete with him, having betrayed her own father for his sake — but on the island of Naxos, where they stopped to rest, Theseus sailed away and left her sleeping on the shore. There the god Dionysus found her abandoned, and took the weeping princess for his own immortal bride.

Theseus took as his wife Phaedra, sister of the Ariadne he had abandoned — but Aphrodite, nursing a grudge, filled Phaedra with a helpless, forbidden love for her stepson Hippolytus, the chaste youth who scorned all women and worshipped only Artemis. Rejected and shamed, Phaedra hanged herself, leaving behind a note accusing Hippolytus of assaulting her. Theseus, believing it, called down a curse of Poseidon that destroyed his innocent son — and learned the truth only too late.

Zeus caught sight of the Phoenician princess Europa gathering flowers by the shore and, to approach her unafraid, took the shape of a magnificent white bull — gentle as a lamb, its breath sweet as saffron. Charmed, Europa wreathed its horns and climbed onto its broad back — whereupon it plunged into the sea and swam, unstoppable, all the way to Crete. There Zeus revealed himself and made her the island's queen; their son Minos would rule it, and the continent she was carried to still bears her name.
Minos, king and later judge of the dead, is a son of Europa by Zeus.
Minos, Zeus's son by Europa, ruled Crete in life and judged the dead after it.

When Minos withheld from Poseidon a magnificent bull meant for sacrifice, the god took a strange revenge: he filled Minos's wife Pasiphae with an unnatural, consuming passion for the animal. Unable to master it, she had the craftsman Daedalus build her a hollow wooden cow in which she could lie concealed — and from that monstrous union she conceived the Minotaur, bull-headed and man-bodied, whom Minos hid away in the Labyrinth that Daedalus built to contain the family's shame.
Pasiphae, cursed to bear the Minotaur, is a daughter of Helios the Sun, and carries her father's uncanny blood.

Cursed by Poseidon to lust after a magnificent white bull, Pasiphae had Daedalus build her a hollow wooden cow to hide inside, and from that monstrous union bore the Minotaur — a creature with a man's body and a bull's head. Her shame was hidden in the Labyrinth Daedalus built, where the beast fed on Athenian tribute until Theseus killed it.
Ariadne, who betrayed her father for Theseus, is a daughter of King Minos.
Phaedra, later wed to Theseus, is a daughter of King Minos.
Ariadne and Phaedra, daughters of Minos, are both drawn into Theseus's orbit and both undone by it.

Abandoned by Theseus and left weeping on the shore of Naxos, Ariadne was found by the god Dionysus, who had fallen in love with her. He took the forsaken princess as his own bride, and where a mortal had betrayed her a god gave her honour: at their wedding he set a crown of gold upon her, and afterward cast it up into the heavens, where it shines still as the constellation Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown.
King Minos kept the craftsman Daedalus on Crete to build the Labyrinth, then imprisoned him to keep its secret.

Imprisoned with his son in the very Labyrinth he had built for King Minos, the master-craftsman Daedalus fashioned two pairs of wings from feathers and wax so they might fly to freedom. He warned Icarus to hold the middle way — not so low the sea's damp would clog the feathers, nor so high the sun would melt the wax. But the boy, drunk on flight, climbed higher and higher, until the wax ran, the feathers scattered, and he fell into the sea that bears his name to this day.
Jason won the Golden Fleece with the help of the sorceress Medea, who betrayed her own father for love of him — a debt he later repaid with a betrayal of his own that destroyed them both.
Medea's magic drugs the guardian dragon and defeats her own father's traps — she saves Jason at every step of the quest.
Medea, who betrays her father for Jason, is the daughter of King Aeetes of Colchis.
Aeetes, keeper of the Golden Fleece, is a son of Helios the Sun and brother of the witch Circe.
King Aeetes set Jason lethal tasks — fire-breathing bulls, warriors sprung from dragon's teeth — meaning the stranger to die trying.

Pelias had seized the throne of Iolcus that rightly belonged to Jason's father, and an oracle had warned him to beware a stranger wearing a single sandal. When Jason arrived just so — having lost one crossing a river — Pelias knew his hour had come. Feigning goodwill, he sent the young man on what he was certain would be a fatal errand: to sail to the world's edge and bring back the Golden Fleece. But Jason returned with the Fleece, and with Medea, whose sorcery would in the end be the death of Pelias himself.

Medea was a priestess of Hecate, goddess of witchcraft, crossroads, and the restless dead, and drew her terrible powers from that patronage. It was by Hecate's arts that Medea brewed the drugs that lulled the dragon guarding the Golden Fleece and the poisons of her later revenge.

Hecate is the dark source behind Medea's story — the goddess who taught a mortal woman magic strong enough to defy kings and murder her own children.
Heracles, mightiest of Jason's Argonauts, left the voyage early to search for a lost companion.
Orpheus sailed with Jason's Argonauts, his music drowning out the Sirens and setting the rowers' stroke.
The huntress Atalanta joined Jason's Argo, the equal on the voyage of any man aboard.
Castor the horseman shipped with his twin among Jason's crew.
Pollux the boxer, who felled the brutal king Amycus, rowed with Jason's Argonauts.
The blind seer Phineus, freed from the tormenting Harpies by Jason's crew, repaid them with the secret of passing the Clashing Rocks.
The winged Harpies snatched or fouled every meal set before the blind prophet Phineus, starving him, until the Argonauts drove them off.
Calliope, chief of the Muses, was mother of Orpheus, giving her son the power to move stones, beasts and even the dead with his song.
Orpheus followed his dead wife Eurydice into the underworld and won her release with his music — only to lose her again by looking back a moment too soon.
The inseparable twins — when mortal Castor died, immortal Pollux gave up half his own immortality to share it, and Zeus set them both in the stars.
Pollux, the immortal twin, was Zeus's son by Leda.
Castor the horseman, the mortal twin, is a son of Leda by her husband.
Pollux the boxer, the immortal twin, is a son of Leda by Zeus in the form of a swan.

Zeus desired Leda, Queen of Sparta, and came to her as a swan, feigning flight from an eagle so that she took the bird to her breast to shelter it. From that union — and from her husband the same night — Leda brought forth eggs, and from them hatched two sets of twins: immortal Pollux and mortal Castor, and the beautiful Helen whose face would burn Troy, alongside Clytemnestra. So a single strange night sowed the seeds of the greatest of wars.
Helen, hatched (the poets said) from an egg, was Leda's daughter by Zeus the swan.
Clytemnestra, Leda's mortal daughter, sister to Helen and the future killer of Agamemnon.
Castor is a brother of Helen, one of the twins who once rescued her from an early abduction.
Clytemnestra and Helen are sisters and dark mirrors — one ran off with a lover and started a war, the other murdered the husband that war kept from home.
Clytemnestra murdered her husband Agamemnon in his bath on his return from Troy, avenging the daughter he had sacrificed to sail there.

Agamemnon had sacrificed their daughter Iphigenia to raise the winds for Troy, and for ten years Clytemnestra nursed her hatred and took his cousin Aegisthus as her lover. When the conquering king came home at last, she welcomed him with false warmth, spread a purple carpet for his feet — then, as he bathed, threw a net over him and struck him down with an axe, and killed the captive prophetess Cassandra beside him. Their son Orestes would one day return to avenge the murdered father upon the murdering mother.

When the great Calydonian Boar ravaged his land, Prince Meleager gathered the finest hunters of Greece to bring it down — among them Atalanta, the fleet-footed huntress raised by a bear, the only woman in the company. Meleager, in love with her, honoured her above the rest: when it was Atalanta who drew first blood on the boar and Meleager who dealt the death-blow, he awarded her the hide. His uncles, insulted that a woman should take the prize, seized it back — and Meleager killed them for it, setting in motion his own doom.
Warned that his son would kill him, King Laius left the infant Oedipus to die; the boy lived, and the prophecy held all the same.
Jocasta gave up her infant to escape the oracle, and years later married the grown stranger Oedipus who was that very son.

An oracle foretold that Oedipus would kill his father and wed his mother, so he fled the couple he believed were his parents, hoping to outrun the prophecy. At a narrow crossroads he quarrelled with a stranger over the right of way and struck him dead — never knowing the man was Laius, King of Thebes, his true father. Thus the first half of the prophecy was fulfilled by the very flight meant to escape it, and Oedipus walked on toward Thebes, and toward his mother's bed.
Oedipus unknowingly married his own mother Jocasta after solving the Sphinx's riddle — a horror that destroyed them both when the truth came to light.
Laius and Jocasta, king and queen of Thebes, who tried to outrun the oracle by killing their own child Oedipus.

The Sphinx — a winged lion with a woman's face — sat outside Thebes and strangled every traveller who failed her riddle: what walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon, and three at evening? Coming to the city a stranger, Oedipus alone answered — Man, who crawls as a babe, strides upright in his prime, and leans on a staff in age. In fury and despair the Sphinx hurled herself from her rock, and grateful Thebes crowned Oedipus its king, and gave him its widowed queen.
Antigone, born of Oedipus's doomed marriage, would herself die defying a king to bury her brother.
Cadmus, founder of Thebes, wed Harmonia in a marriage attended by all the gods — but her cursed necklace doomed their line to generations of grief.
Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, married Cadmus the founder of Thebes.
Aphrodite's daughter Harmonia married Cadmus in a rare gathering of every god.

Sent to his death against the Chimera — a fire-breathing horror, lion in front, serpent behind, a goat's head rising from its spine — Bellerophon first had to master the winged horse Pegasus, which Athena helped him bridle at a spring. Mounted and airborne, safe above the flames, he rained arrows down upon the beast, then drove a lump of lead into its throat on his spear-point; the monster's own fire melted the metal, and the molten flood seared its innards until it died.
Bellerophon tamed the winged horse Pegasus with Athena's golden bridle and rode him to kill the Chimera from the air — before pride sent him tumbling from the same steed.
Some make Bellerophon a son of Poseidon — the sea-god's blood behind his winged conquest.
Gaia raised her monstrous last-born Typhon against the Olympians who had chained her Titan sons.
Typhon, storm-monster of a hundred dragon-heads, was sired on Gaia by Tartarus the abyss as a last assault on Zeus.
Typhon, father of monsters, mated with Echidna, mother of monsters; their brood terrorised the whole age of heroes.

When the Olympians had cast down the Titans, Gaia bore one last and greatest monster to overthrow them: Typhon, a hundred-headed storm-giant whose roars were the cries of every beast and whose reach brushed the stars. The other gods fled to Egypt in animal shapes, but Zeus stood alone. After a battle that shook the world — and one dark hour when Typhon cut out his sinews and left him crippled — Zeus recovered, drove the monster back beneath a storm of thunderbolts, and buried him under Mount Etna, whose eruptions are his fury still.

Typhon rose against Zeus to seize the cosmos, and in their battle briefly tore the sinews from the god's limbs — until Zeus recovered, felled him with a storm of thunderbolts, and pinned him beneath Mount Etna.
The Lernaean Hydra that Heracles faced is a child of Echidna, mother of monsters.
Echidna's fire-breathing daughter, the lion-goat-serpent Chimera.
Cerberus, the three-headed hound of Hades, is a child of Echidna and Typhon.
The riddling Sphinx was Echidna's daughter, sent to plague Thebes.
The impenetrable lion of Nemea was another of Echidna's brood.
Ladon, the hundred-headed dragon of the golden apples, is a child of Echidna.
Typhon's fire lived on in his daughter the Chimera.
The hound Cerberus counted the storm-monster Typhon as his sire.
Cerberus lets every shade into the underworld and none back out — the perfect servant of Hades.
Gaia the Earth bore the serpent Python, who guarded the oracle at Delphi before Apollo came.

Python, a monstrous serpent, guarded the sacred spring at the navel of the earth, and had once hounded Apollo's mother Leto across the world at Hera's command. Still a young god, Apollo climbed the slopes of Parnassus and slew the great snake with his silver bow, seizing its oracle for his own. There he founded Delphi, and named its prophetess the Pythia in the dead serpent's honour — the most sacred voice in all of Greece.
Freed by Zeus from Tartarus, the Cyclopes repaid him by forging the thunderbolts that won the war against the Titans.
The Cyclopes, one-eyed giant smiths, are children of Gaia the Earth and Uranus the Sky.
Uranus feared and imprisoned his Cyclopes children deep in the earth, until Zeus freed them to forge his thunderbolts.
Hundred-eyed Argus never slept with more than half his eyes at once — the perfect watchman for Hera's jealous purposes.

When Zeus turned his lover Io into a white heifer to hide her, jealous Hera set the hundred-eyed giant Argus Panoptes to guard her — a watchman who never truly slept, for only some of his eyes ever closed at once. Zeus sent Hermes to free her, and the god lulled all hundred eyes to sleep with the drowsy music of his pipes and a long dull tale, then struck off the giant's head. In his memory, Hera set Argus's hundred eyes into the tail of her peacock.

Eros, the god of desire, is most often called the son of Aphrodite, and works as the instrument of his mother's power — loosing the arrows that make gods and mortals fall helplessly in love. Where Aphrodite is beauty and longing itself, Eros is the sharp, sudden strike of it, mother and son together ruling the whole domain of love.
Hermes fathered the goat-legged Pan, wild god of the shepherds' hills.
Iris the rainbow carries the messages of Hera between heaven, earth and sea.
Winged Nike, Victory, stands at the side of Zeus — the outcome he grants to whom he favours.
The daughter of Zeus and Hera, Hebe poured the nectar of the gods as their cupbearer before she was given in marriage to the deified Heracles.
Hera's daughter Hebe, whose eternal youth she would later bestow on the deified Heracles as his bride.
Eris, Strife, and Ares, War, are siblings who walk the battlefield side by side.
Nemesis answered the prayers of everyone Narcissus spurned — luring him to the still pool where he'd fall for his own reflection.

The nymph Echo, cursed by Hera to speak only the last words she heard, fell hopelessly in love with the beautiful youth Narcissus — yet could only echo his own words back, and he spurned her cruelly. She wasted away in grief until nothing remained of her but a voice. In punishment Narcissus was made to fall in love with his own reflection in a still pool, and there he pined away, unable to leave the image he could never hold, until he too withered into the flower that bears his name.
Eos the Dawn is a daughter of the Titan Hyperion and Theia.
Theia bore Eos, the rosy-fingered Dawn.

Eos the rosy-fingered Dawn and Helios the Sun are siblings, children of the Titans Hyperion and Theia. Each morning Eos rises first from the eastern sea and throws open the gates of the sky, and her brother's blazing chariot follows the path she has opened — dawn forever going before the day.

Eos the Dawn and Selene the Moon are sisters, daughters of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, and between them and their brother Helios the three divide the light of the sky. Selene drives her silver chariot through the night; Eos rises to end it, throwing open the eastern gates so that the darkness her sister ruled gives way to her brother's day.
Selene the Moon is a daughter of the Titan Hyperion, sister to the Sun and the Dawn.
Theia bore Selene, the Moon.
Helios the Sun and Selene the Moon, brother and sister, cross the heavens in turn.
Apollo fathered Asclepius and gave him to the wise centaur Chiron to raise — under whom the boy mastered a healing art that would one day rival death itself.
The wise centaur Chiron taught Asclepius medicine so thoroughly that the pupil learned to cheat death itself.

Asclepius, son of Apollo, grew so skilled in medicine that he could raise the dead — and when he did, Zeus saw the order of the world itself threatened, for if no one died the balance between gods and mortals would break. With a single thunderbolt he struck the healer down. Grief-stricken and enraged, Apollo could not touch Zeus, so he killed the Cyclopes who forged the bolt — and for that was sentenced to a year's servitude to a mortal king. Asclepius was later set among the stars.
Hypnos, gentle Sleep, is a son of Nyx the Night.
Thanatos, Death, is a son of Nyx the Night and twin brother of Sleep.
Hypnos and Thanatos, Sleep and Death, are twin sons of Night — one a nightly rehearsal for the other.
Zeus fathered the nine Muses on Memory; Calliope, of epic song, was the eldest.
Calliope, chief of the Muses, is a daughter of Mnemosyne, Memory, by Zeus.
The three Fates, the Moirai, are daughters of Nyx the Night, outranking even the gods in the matter of destiny.
Chiron was Cronus's son by a nymph — which set him apart from the wild, violent centaurs as the wise and immortal one.
Chiron fed the boy Achilles on lions' marrow and taught him war, medicine and music alike.
Chiron reared the exiled child Jason on Mount Pelion and schooled him for the throne he'd return to claim.

Ganymede, a Trojan prince, was the most beautiful of all mortal youths — so lovely that Zeus himself was smitten. In the form of a great eagle the god swept down and carried the boy up to Olympus, where he was made immortal and given the honoured office of cupbearer to the gods, pouring their nectar in Hebe's place. To his grieving father Zeus sent divine horses in recompense, and set Ganymede's likeness among the stars as the constellation Aquarius.
Zeus loved the priestess Io and, to hide her from Hera, turned her into a white heifer — which only began her sufferings.

Io was a priestess of Hera whom Zeus desired; caught in the act of seduction, Zeus turned her into a white heifer to hide the affair. But Hera, unfooled, demanded the heifer as a gift and set the hundred-eyed Argus to guard her. Even when Hermes killed the watchman and freed her, Hera sent a maddening gadfly to sting the heifer on and on, driving poor Io in torment across the whole world — a wandering that gave its name to the Ionian Sea and the Bosphorus, the 'ox-ford', before she found rest at last in Egypt.
Hundred-eyed Argus was set to watch the transformed Io night and day, so Zeus could never reach her.
Struck by Eros's arrow, Apollo pursued the nymph Daphne, who fled and was turned into a laurel tree — whose leaves the god took ever after as his crown.
Iapetus fathered Epimetheus, the heedless Titan whose afterthought left mankind defenceless and who took the fatal Pandora as his bride.
Prometheus and Epimetheus, Forethought and Afterthought, are brothers — one steals fire and foresees the cost, the other opens the door to Pandora.
Ignoring Prometheus's warning to refuse any gift from the gods, Epimetheus took Pandora as his wife — and her jar did the rest.
At Zeus's command, Hephaestus moulded Pandora, the first woman, from clay — beautiful, and bearing the jar of every human ill, the gods' revenge for stolen fire.

So cunning was Sisyphus that when Death came for him he asked Thanatos to show how his own chains worked — then snapped them shut, and no mortal died anywhere on earth until Ares came to free him. Caught again, Sisyphus had told his wife to leave his corpse unburied, then talked Persephone into letting him return briefly to rebuke her — and simply refused to go back. For cheating death twice he was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever, only to watch it roll back each time it neared the crest.

Tantalus, a son of Zeus admitted to the tables of the gods, betrayed that honour again and again — stealing their nectar and ambrosia for mortals, and, worst of all, killing his own son Pelops and serving him up as a feast to test whether the gods could tell. They knew at once. Their punishment was eternal: set in a pool that drained away whenever he bent to drink, beneath fruit that the wind swung out of reach whenever he grasped — forever hungry, forever thirsty, forever tantalised.
Grateful for a kindness, Dionysus granted Midas the golden touch — then, hearing his misery, mercifully took it back.
The sculptor Pygmalion loved his own ivory statue so purely that Aphrodite gave it life as the woman Galatea.
Moved by his devotion, Aphrodite answered Pygmalion's prayer and gave his ivory statue a beating heart.

When Poseidon sought the sea-nymph Amphitrite for his queen, she fled him into the farthest deeps of the ocean, wanting nothing to do with the god. But a dolphin found her hiding place and pleaded Poseidon's cause so sweetly that she relented and consented to be his bride. In gratitude Poseidon set the dolphin among the stars as a constellation, and Amphitrite reigned beside him as queen of the sea, mother of the merman Triton.
Aether the bright air is the child of Nyx the Night and her brother Erebus — light born, strangely, out of darkness.
Hemera the Day is Night's own daughter: as Nyx leaves the sky each dawn, Hemera enters it, and they never share it.
Aether the upper air and Hemera the Day are paired as the bright powers of the heavens, children together of the primordial dark.
Gaia the Earth brought forth Ourea, the mountains, from herself alone, as she did the sea and sky.
Nereus, the gentle 'Old Man of the Sea', is the eldest son of Pontus the Deep and Gaia the Earth.
Phorcys, god of the sea's hidden perils, is a son of Pontus the Deep and Gaia.
Ceto, mother of sea-monsters, is a daughter of Pontus the Deep and Gaia the Earth.
Phorcys and his sister Ceto together spawned the sea's monstrous brood — the Gorgons, the Graeae and the serpent Echidna among them.
Medusa the Gorgon is a daughter of the sea-gods Phorcys and Ceto.
Ceto, goddess of sea-monsters, mothered the Gorgon Medusa with Phorcys.
The grey Graeae are daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, sisters and wardens of their kin the Gorgons.
Ceto bore the Graeae, three grey sisters with a single shared eye, alongside her Gorgon daughters.
Nereus, the truthful old man of the sea, fathered the fifty Nereids — Thetis, mother of Achilles, chief among them.
Amphitrite, queen of the sea, is a Nereid daughter of Nereus.
Triton the merman is the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, herald of his father's sea.
Proteus the shape-shifting seer serves Poseidon as herdsman of his seals in the deep.
Styx, eldest of the underworld rivers, is a daughter of the Titan Oceanus and Tethys.
Tethys mothered the river-goddess Styx, whose waters bind even the gods' oaths.
When Zeus rose against the Titans, Styx was the first to bring her children to his side; in thanks he made her name the oath no god dares break.
Crius the Titan of the constellations is a son of Uranus the Sky and Gaia the Earth.
Gaia bore the Titan Crius, whose line would include the stars, the winds and the dawn.
Menoetius the violent is a son of Iapetus, and brother to Atlas and Prometheus.
The Oceanid Clymene bore Menoetius to Iapetus, alongside Atlas and Prometheus.
For his reckless violence in the war of the gods, Zeus struck Menoetius down with a thunderbolt into the dark of Erebus.
The Titan Iapetus and the Oceanid Clymene are the parents of Prometheus, Atlas and Epimetheus.
Prometheus the forethinker is the son of Iapetus and the Oceanid Clymene.
Atlas, who holds up the sky, is a son of Iapetus and Clymene.
Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, is the daughter of Zeus and Hera — and the very help Hera withholds from Zeus's other loves in labour.
Hera's daughter Eileithyia eases childbirth; Hera commands her to delay the births of her husband's rivals.
Deimos, Terror, is the son of Ares the war-god and Aphrodite, and rides at his father's side into battle.
Aphrodite bore Deimos, Terror, to Ares — love and war together fathering panic.
Phobos, Fear, is a son of Ares and Aphrodite, the dread that scatters armies before his father.
Aphrodite mothered Phobos, Fear, with the war-god Ares.
Deimos and Phobos, Terror and Fear, are twin sons of Ares and Aphrodite who haunt every battlefield together.
Morpheus, who shapes the figures of dreams, is a son of Hypnos the Sleep.
The Furies sprang from the blood of Uranus when Cronus unmanned him — vengeance itself born of that first violence.
Charon ferries the dead across the Styx into the realm of Hades, taking his fee in the coins left with the dead.
The three Graces, who lend beauty and joy, are daughters of Zeus.
The Graces attend Aphrodite, dressing and adorning the goddess of beauty as her constant companions.
Stheno the immortal Gorgon is a daughter of the sea-gods Phorcys and Ceto, and sister to Medusa.
Euryale the immortal Gorgon is Ceto's daughter and Medusa's sister.
Stheno and Euryale are Medusa's deathless Gorgon sisters; only Medusa could be slain, and Perseus slew her.
Euryale is Medusa's immortal sister, whose wail of grief follows Perseus's killing stroke.
Stheno and Euryale, the two immortal Gorgons, guard the memory of their slain sister Medusa.

To find the road to Medusa, Perseus first had to wring the secret from the Graeae — three grey witches, sisters of the Gorgons, old since birth, who shared a single eye and a single tooth between them, passing them from hand to hand. Perseus watched and waited, and at the very moment the eye was being handed across, he snatched it away. Blind and helpless, the sisters could only bargain: to win back their one eye they told him where to find the nymphs who kept the weapons he would need.
The grey Graeae kept the secret road to their sisters the Gorgons, Medusa among them, until Perseus forced it from them.

For his tenth labour Heracles journeyed to the far western edge of the world to seize the cattle of Geryon — a monster with three bodies joined at the waist, three heads, six arms. To reach him he crossed the ocean in the golden cup of the Sun, and on the way raised the great Pillars that bear his name at the strait. He slew the herdsman and the two-headed hound Orthrus, then felled Geryon with a single arrow, poisoned with the Hydra's blood, that pierced all three bodies at once.

Orthrus was a two-headed hound — brother to Cerberus, born of the monsters Typhon and Echidna — set to guard the red cattle of Geryon at the western edge of the world. When Heracles came to carry off the herd for his tenth labour, the beast rushed him, and he felled it with a single blow of his olivewood club before turning on its master. It was the first of the guardians of Geryon's cattle to fall.
The two-headed dog Orthrus guarded the cattle of the giant Geryon until Heracles came for the herd.
Orthrus the two-headed hound is another of Echidna's monstrous brood, brother to Cerberus.

For his fourth labour Heracles was ordered to bring the monstrous Erymanthian Boar back alive — a beast that ravaged the mountain slopes. He chased it up into the high snows, where its heavy body floundered in the drifts, then sprang upon it, bound it fast in chains, and hauled it onto his shoulders. When he carried the living, thrashing boar into the court of King Eurystheus, who had set him the labours, the terrified king dived into a great bronze jar to hide and shouted his orders from inside it.

For his sixth labour Heracles faced the Stymphalian Birds — a vast flock of man-eating creatures with bronze beaks, metallic feathers they could loose like arrows, and poisonous dung, that had gathered in a marsh too soft to cross on foot or by boat. Athena gave him a great bronze rattle forged by Hephaestus; its clashing din startled the birds up into the air in a screaming cloud, and there Heracles shot them down with his arrows as they flew, and drove the survivors from Greece forever.

The third labour asked not for slaughter but for patience: to capture the Ceryneian Hind alive, a deer sacred to Artemis with golden antlers and hooves of bronze, swifter than an arrow. Unwilling to harm a creature of the goddess, Heracles pursued it on foot for a full year, across mountains and rivers to the edge of the world, until at last he caught it — and when Artemis rose in anger to stop him, he explained the labour laid on him, and she let him carry the hind away unhurt.
The golden Hind is sacred to Artemis, who nearly punishes Heracles until he shows he took it alive and unharmed.

For his seventh labour Heracles sailed to Crete to capture the great Bull that Poseidon had sent from the sea — the same beast that had fathered the Minotaur upon Queen Pasiphae, and now ran wild ravaging the island. King Minos offered help, but Heracles took it alone: he wrestled the raging bull down with his bare hands, subdued it, and shipped it back across the water to Greece. Released afterward, it wandered north to the plain of Marathon, to trouble heroes yet to come.
The Cretan Bull, sent by Poseidon, rampaged over Minos's Crete until Heracles removed it.
Poseidon sent the Cretan Bull ashore; when Minos failed to sacrifice it, the god turned it wild.
Telamon fought beside Heracles in an earlier sack of Troy and sailed with him among the Argonauts.

Tantalus, testing whether the gods were truly all-knowing, killed his son Pelops, cooked him, and served the flesh at a feast. The gods saw through it at once and refused the meal — all but grieving Demeter, who absently ate the shoulder. They restored Pelops to life and gave him a shoulder of gleaming ivory to replace the eaten piece, while Tantalus was damned to his eternal hunger and thirst in the underworld.

Pelops, as a boy, had been served up by his father Tantalus as a meal to test the gods — and though the others recoiled, Demeter distractedly ate his shoulder. The gods restored the boy to life, fashioning a shoulder of ivory to replace the eaten one, and he emerged more beautiful than before. So lovely was he that Poseidon fell in love with him, carried him up to Olympus, and later, when Pelops raced for a bride, gave him a chariot drawn by winged horses to win her.
Atreus, whose house the family curse would tear apart, is a son of Pelops.
Thyestes, rival to his brother Atreus, is a son of Pelops.
Atreus took revenge on his brother Thyestes by serving him his own murdered sons at a banquet — the crime at the black heart of their house's curse.
Atreus took revenge on his brother Thyestes by serving him a feast of his own murdered sons.
Agamemnon, who leads the Greeks to Troy, is a son of Atreus of Mycenae.
Menelaus, whose wife Helen was carried to Troy, is a son of Atreus and brother of Agamemnon.
Aegisthus, who murders Agamemnon, is the surviving son of Thyestes — the family's revenge made flesh.
While Agamemnon warred at Troy, Aegisthus became the lover of his wife Clytemnestra and her partner in his murder.
Aegisthus, avenging his father Thyestes, helps Clytemnestra cut down Agamemnon on his return from Troy.
Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to win fair winds for Troy — the crime that turned his wife into his murderer.

Becalmed at Aulis, the Greek fleet could not sail for Troy until Agamemnon appeased Artemis — and the price the goddess named was his own daughter.
